extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on NLP / ML for patent analysis (patent retrieval, classification, IE, novelty/granting/litigation prediction)
extracted.subtask_description: A survey-style rubric describing definitions, evaluation methods, dataset considerations, and methodological desiderata for automated patent tasks including subject classification, retrieval (prior-art/landscaping/FTO), information extraction, and quality assessment (novelty, granting, litigation, valuation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent subject classification task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The automated subject classification task is a multi-label classification task. The aim is to predict patents’ specific categories or classes based on patent content, including title, abstract, and claims. Given inputs x = [w1, w2, ..., wn], the objective is to predict label y ∈ {y1, y2, ..., ym}; since patents may belong to multiple classes, sometimes more than one label needs predicting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial for organizing patent databases, facilitating patent searches, and assisting examiners in evaluating novelty. Use multi-label modelling approaches and consider inputs from title, abstract, claims (and potentially full descriptions) to capture class information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methods for patent classification (Fall et al., 2003)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three mainstream evaluation methods: top prediction, top N guesses, and all categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top prediction checks whether the top-1 prediction matches the main class. Top N guesses is successful if one of the top-n predictions matches the main class (more flexible). All-categories checks whether the top-1 prediction is included in the set of the main class and all incidental classes. Choose method according to task needs (strict vs flexible evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Common metrics reported include precision (P), accuracy (A), F1 score, and mean average precision (MAP) for retrieval-like setups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report multiple metrics (precision, recall/F1, accuracy, MAP) as appropriate for multi-label and ranking evaluations. The paper shows precision commonly used for top-prediction results; MAP is used for retrieval-oriented comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three methodological paradigms for patent classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Main categories of methods are: (1) feature extraction and classifier, (2) fine-tuning transformer-based language models, and (3) hybrid methods (multimodal, multi-view, ensembles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature-extraction approaches use embeddings (bag-of-words, GloVe, Word2Vec, FastText, GPT-2) with classifiers (CNN/RNN/KNN). Fine-tuning transformers (BERT, XLNet, RoBERTa, ELECTRA) often outperform traditional methods. Hybrid methods combine modalities (text, images, graphs) or ensemble multiple models to improve robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parts of patent documents for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical inputs for classification models are title, abstract, and claims; many studies focus on short texts (abstracts and claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles and abstracts are generic and may lack detailed information; the paper recommends future work to focus on full descriptions which contain more specific technical information. Consider which patent fields to include depending on task and model capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-adaptive training and domain-specific embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain-specific word embeddings and domain-adaptive pre-training improve classification performance compared to off-the-shelf embeddings trained on heterogeneous corpora.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train or adapt embeddings on patent corpora (domain-adaptive pre-training, adapters) to capture patent-specific terminology; experiments report ~2–4% improvements in some settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for standard benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers use different datasets and metrics, which complicates comparison of methods; the paper calls for standard benchmarks for patent classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt shared datasets, consistent splits and metrics to enable fair comparisons; use curated patent datasets (e.g., USPTO-2M, HUPD) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-n vs top-1 reporting for classification results
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting top-1 (top prediction) is stricter; top-n reporting (top N guesses) is more flexible and can reflect practical utility when multiple candidate classes are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both top-1 and top-n metrics when relevant; clarify whether evaluation checks main class only or includes incidental classes (all-categories method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence-to-sequence approach for hierarchical classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating hierarchical classification as a sequence generation task (outputting full IPC/CPC code sequence) was attempted but produced mediocre accuracy (e.g., 56.7% in tested datasets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence generation for fine-grained hierarchical labels is possible but may underperform; consider trade-offs versus classification models tailored to hierarchical outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent retrieval (prior-art search) task definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior-art search: given a target patent document X, automatically retrieve K documents most relevant to X from a patent database to assist examiners in assessing patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success measured by retrieval quality metrics (MAP, precision@k, etc.). Handle domain-specific terminology and invented terms that differ from common language; consider cross-domain documents that may be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyword-based / statistical retrieval baseline considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional retrieval methods include keyword-based search and statistical ranking algorithms such as BM25 and TF-IDF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keyword methods are straightforward but suffer from terminology variation and invented terms. Use query-expansion, query-reduction, or hybrid methods to mitigate synonymy/terminology issues. BM25 is a strong baseline and should be compared against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-text and document-level embedding retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving from keyword/short-text to full-text retrieval and using document-level embeddings (e.g., Doc2Vec) can substantially improve retrieval performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full-text similarity search captures more context and can yield better results than title/abstract-only approaches. Document-level embeddings often outperform word-level embeddings for retrieval tasks; consider training embeddings on patent corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep-learning embeddings and transformer-based retrieval caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep-learning-based embeddings (Word2Vec variants, BERT-based paragraph/document models) are explored; some transformer-based retrieval models (e.g., BERT-PLI) did not surpass BM25 in certain patent retrieval experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate transformer-based retrieval vs robust baselines like BM25 on patent corpora; incorporate global context or paragraph-level interactions where useful, but validate gains empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrieval-augmented LLMs as a research direction
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrating retrieval into LLMs (retrieval-augmented generation) can improve factual accuracy and downstream performance in text retrieval and QA tasks; promising for patent prior-art search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate RAG architectures and retrieval-augmented LMs for patent search and QA; ensure retrieval component is tailored to patent corpora and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent landscaping task definition and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent landscaping aims to retrieve patent documents related to a particular topic for strategic analysis; methods include keyword-based retrieval or seed-patent-based retrieval; classification models can be trained to decide topic membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landscaping can be framed as retrieval or binary classification. Use seed patents to expand topical sets or train topic classifiers using text and graph features (e.g., concatenated embeddings of abstracts and subject-category graph embeddings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom-to-operate (FTO) search definition and core requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom-to-operate search determines if a product/technology would be covered by active IP rights. It differs from prior-art novelty search by focusing on active patents/applications and whether independent claims cover the technology (claims with fewer features covering broader scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTO requires detailed claim analysis and automated retrieval of targeted patent claims; design systems to retrieve and compare specific claim language to the technology's feature set. This is underexplored and recommended for future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information extraction (IE) task definition in patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Information extraction transforms patent text into structured data (entities, relations, knowledge graphs) to support downstream applications such as analysis, recommendation, and engineering design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between rule-based (transparent, precise, but costly to maintain) and deep-learning-based methods (scalable, flexible, require labeled data). For long descriptions, use models that can handle long context (e.g., encoder-decoder T5 variants or specialized long-context transformers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based vs deep-learning IE trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule-based systems use hand-crafted patterns for precise and interpretable extraction but are time-consuming and brittle. Deep-learning methods (LSTM, transformers) can handle varied language expressions but require annotated datasets and compute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rule-based methods for high-precision, well-scoped extraction needs; use DL methods when large annotated data and compute are available and when language variability demands learning. Hybrid approaches may combine benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: IE applications and target evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: IE outputs support patent analysis (novelty/quality assessment), patent recommendation (company-patent relations), and engineering design (extracting problems/solutions/advantages). Report task-specific metrics (e.g., F1 for entity/relation extraction; accuracy for classification of motivations/specifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide downstream evaluation: e.g., Giordano et al. obtained F1=90% for extracting technical problems/solutions; report standard IE metrics and validate utility in downstream tasks like recommendation or forecasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality assessment dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality assessment covers novelty prediction, granting prediction, litigation prediction, and patent valuation as measures reflecting patent quality and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty prediction helps pre-filing assessment; granting prediction models whether the office will grant an application (considering formal language/figures/documents); litigation prediction estimates odds of future litigation (ambiguous claims increase risk); valuation quantifies economic worth. Use appropriate labeled datasets and combine textual, metadata and procedural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics for labeling novelty in datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of heuristics: Arts et al. (2021) considered patents connected to awards (e.g., Nobel Prize) as novel; patents granted by the USPTO but rejected by both EPO and JPO were labeled as lacking novelty. The authors caution these heuristics may deviate from formal novelty definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about labeling heuristics and limitations; where possible prefer domain-expert labels or more formal novelty definitions. Recognize such proxies may introduce biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset standards and gold vs silver labels for text generation tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-written texts are the gold standard for text-generation tasks. For patent simplification, obtaining gold-standard simplified texts is expensive; Casola et al. (2023) used automated tools to create a silver standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gold human annotations when feasible; when using silver standards (automatically generated), clearly document generation process and limitations. Use large multipurpose datasets (e.g., HUPD) for many tasks but verify label quality per task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal and ensemble approaches for improved performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimodal models (text + images + graphs) and ensemble methods that combine multiple classifiers can achieve higher accuracy and robustness than unimodal single models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patent documents that include figures/images and relational metadata, leverage multimodal architectures (CNNs for images, RNNs/transformers for text, GNNs for relations). Use ensembles to reduce variance and bias; validate gains against single strong baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection ease and label availability for classification tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Because granted patents are assigned classification codes and contain referenced patents, researchers can collect and filter patents to formulate datasets without additional labeling for subject classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit existing IPC/CPC labels for supervised training but be mindful of label granularity/hierarchy. Provide clear train/validation/test splits and document parts used (title, abstract, claims, full text).
